route1.name: Chengdu Tibetan Walking Tour
route1.tagline: Tibetan culture hidden inside the city
route1.description: A two-hour introduction to Tibetan culture hidden inside the city — temples, tea houses, and living traditions most visitors never find.

itinerary.title: Meet & Greet
itinerary.desc: Meet at Gaoshengqiao Metro Station Exit G. Get to know your guide and fellow travelers.

itinerary.title: Tibetan Quarter Walk
itinerary.desc: Stroll through Chengdu's most authentic Tibetan neighborhood — temples, prayer wheels, traditional dress, and daily life woven together in the city.

itinerary.title: Tibetan Tea & Snacks
itinerary.desc: Step into a traditional Tibetan tea house. Taste authentic butter tea or sweet tea alongside Tibetan snacks, while listening to stories of the plateau.

itinerary.title: Tibetan Guozhuang Dance
itinerary.desc: Watch a traditional Guozhuang circle dance performance — the rhythm and warmth of highland culture. Return to the meeting point afterward.

faq.q: Do I need a guide who speaks my language?
faq.a: Our city walk runs in English by default. Spanish and Thai guides can be arranged on request — just tell us your dates and language when you enquire.

faq.q: Is this walk suitable for children or older travellers?
faq.a: Yes. It is a gentle two-hour walk on flat city streets with plenty of stops for tea and rest. There are no steep steps, though the temple courtyards have some uneven paving.

faq.q: What happens if it rains?
faq.a: The walk runs in light rain and we adjust the route to stay under cover where possible. In the event of serious weather we will reschedule or refund in full.

faq.q: Can I join if I have dietary restrictions?
faq.a: Absolutely. Tell us in advance and we will arrange alternative snacks — the butter tea can also be swapped for sweet tea, which contains no dairy in the way butter tea does.

faq.q: How do I get to the meeting point?
faq.a: We meet at Gaoshengqiao Metro Station Exit G, which is on Line 3. Your guide will be holding a Chengdu Journeys sign. We will send the exact location on WhatsApp the day before.

route2.name: Highland Roads & Temple Views
route2.tagline: Escape the city into Sichuan's highlands
route2.description: Escape the city and explore highland roads, ancient temples, and mountain panoramas across the Tibetan plateau's eastern edge.

days.title: Chengdu → Kangding
days.desc: Depart Chengdu in the afternoon, cross the Erlang Mountain Tunnel via the Yakang Expressway, and arrive in Kangding — capital of Ganzi Prefecture — by evening. Stroll along the Zheduo River and soak in the Tibetan atmosphere of this legendary gateway town.

days.title: S434 · Muya Monastery · Yala Snow Mountain → Xinduqiao
days.desc: Take the stunning Provincial Road 434 north — quieter and more scenic than the main G318. Visit Muya Monastery, where golden roofs and crimson walls frame snow peaks and grasslands. Stop at the Yala Snow Mountain viewpoint to face the majesty of this sacred peak. Arrive in Xinduqiao by dusk — known as 'photographer's paradise' for its dreamlike play of light on Tibetan villages and poplar forests.

days.title: Zheduo Pass → Chengdu
days.desc: Cross Zheduo Pass (4,298m) — the first major pass on the Sichuan-Tibet highway — surrounded by prayer flags and snow peaks. Continue via Kangding back to Chengdu, arriving in the evening.

days.title: Chengdu → Kangding
days.desc: Depart Chengdu in the afternoon, cross the Erlang Mountain Tunnel via the Yakang Expressway, and arrive in Kangding by evening. Stroll along the Zheduo River and soak in the Tibetan atmosphere.

days.title: S434 · Muya Monastery · Yala Snow Mountain → Xinduqiao
days.desc: Take the stunning Provincial Road 434 north. Visit Muya Monastery — golden roofs and crimson walls against snow peaks. Stop at the Yala Snow Mountain viewpoint. Arrive in Xinduqiao by dusk, where light and shadow paint the Tibetan villages and poplar groves.

days.title: Tagong Grasslands · Bamei → Zhonglu Tibetan Village
days.desc: Morning walk on the Tagong Grasslands, where Muya Golden Pagoda frames Yala Snow Mountain. Continue through Bamei into Danba county. Arrive at Zhonglu Tibetan Village — a thousand-year-old Gyalrong settlement of watchtowers, pear blossoms (in spring), and terraced fields. Explore ancient watchtowers and Tibetan homes in the afternoon.

days.title: Zhonglu Village → Chengdu
days.desc: Wake up in the village as morning mist wraps around the watchtowers — Zhonglu's most magical hour. After a morning of free exploration, head back toward Chengdu via the Siguniang Mountain route (distant view from Maobiliang Pass), arriving in the evening.

days.title: Chengdu → Kangding
days.desc: Depart Chengdu in the afternoon, cross the Erlang Mountain Tunnel, and arrive in Kangding by evening. Stroll along the Zheduo River and soak in the Tibetan atmosphere of this legendary gateway town.

days.title: S434 · Muya Monastery · Yala Snow Mountain → Xinduqiao
days.desc: Take stunning Provincial Road 434 north. Visit Muya Monastery, where golden roofs frame snow peaks. Stop at the Yala Snow Mountain viewpoint before arriving in Xinduqiao — photographer's paradise — by dusk.

days.title: Tagong · Bamei · Moshi Park → Danba
days.desc: Morning on the Tagong Grasslands — Muya Golden Pagoda and Yala Snow Mountain in one frame. Continue to Moshi Park near Bamei, where bizarre mylonite stone forests spread across the plateau like an alien landscape. Afternoon drive through the Yak Valley natural bonsai corridor to Danba.

days.title: Danba · Zhonglu Village → Siguniang Mountain
days.desc: Morning exploration of Zhonglu Tibetan Village — a thousand-year-old Gyalrong settlement of watchtowers and stone homes. Visit ancient watchtowers and meet local families. Afternoon drive to Siguniang Mountain, with a panoramic stop at Maobiliang Pass to view all four sacred peaks.

days.title: Siguniang Mountain → Chengdu
days.desc: Morning visit to Shuangqiao Valley — ride the shuttle deep into the valley, passing snow peaks, alpine meadows, and glacial lakes. Afternoon return to Chengdu via Balang Mountain and Wolong Nature Reserve, arriving in the evening.

days.title: Chengdu → Kangding
days.desc: Depart Chengdu in the afternoon, cross the Erlang Mountain Tunnel, and arrive in Kangding by evening. Stroll along the Zheduo River and soak in the Tibetan atmosphere.

days.title: S434 · Muya Monastery · Yala Snow Mountain → Xinduqiao
days.desc: Take stunning Provincial Road 434 north. Visit Muya Monastery — golden roofs and crimson walls against snow peaks. Stop at the Yala Snow Mountain viewpoint, then arrive in Xinduqiao by dusk.

days.title: Tagong · Bamei · Moshi Park → Danba
days.desc: Morning on the Tagong Grasslands — Muya Golden Pagoda and Yala Snow Mountain in one frame. Continue to Moshi Park, where bizarre mylonite stone forests spread across the plateau. Afternoon through the Yak Valley to Danba.

days.title: Zhonglu Village — Full Day Immersion
days.desc: A full day immersed in Zhonglu Tibetan Village — watchtowers emerging from morning mist, pear blossoms weaving through stone homes. Hike to the No. 1 viewpoint for a sweeping panorama. Visit a Tibetan family for butter tea and stories of Gyalrong history. Climb the tallest ancient watchtower for sunset.

days.title: Jiaju Tibetan Village → Siguniang Mountain
days.desc: Morning visit to Jiaju Tibetan Village — 'China's most beautiful village' — where stone homes cascade down the mountainside in harmony with forest and field. Afternoon drive to Siguniang Mountain for the panoramic view of all four peaks from Maobiliang Pass.

days.title: Siguniang Shuangqiao Valley — Full Day
days.desc: A full day in Shuangqiao Valley — ride the shuttle deep into the valley from Renshenguo Meadow to Redwood Forest. Snow peaks, glaciers, alpine forests, meadows, and lakes unfold mile after mile. Optional light hikes at Bonsai Beach or beneath Budala Peak.

days.title: Siguniang Mountain → Chengdu
days.desc: One last look at Siguniang's golden sunrise (weather permitting), then return to Chengdu via Balang Mountain Tunnel and Wolong Nature Reserve, arriving in the afternoon.

faq.q: Which itinerary length should I choose?
faq.a: Three days covers Kangding, Xinduqiao and Zheduo Pass — good if your time is short. Four to five days adds Tagong and Danba, which is what most guests choose. Seven days includes Siguniang Mountain and gives you a full day in Zhonglu village without rushing.

faq.q: How high do we go, and is altitude a problem?
faq.a: The highest point is Zheduo Pass at 4,298 m, which we cross by vehicle rather than sleeping at. Overnight stops sit between 2,560 m and 3,700 m. We climb gradually, and your vehicle carries oxygen.

faq.q: What is the road like?
faq.a: Main roads are paved and generally in good condition. Provincial Road 434 and some village sections are narrower with more bends but are perfectly manageable in a private vehicle. Landslides after heavy rain can close sections briefly; we monitor conditions and reroute if needed.

faq.q: Can this route be customised?
faq.a: Yes — all our highland routes are built to order. Tell us your dates, how many days you have and what you most want to see, and we will put together an itinerary around it.

faq.q: When is the best time to travel?
faq.a: Late May to early October for reliable roads and green grasslands. Mid-October onwards brings the autumn colour but colder nights. Winter travel is possible, though some high passes may close after snow.

route3.name: Nomad Between Earth & Sky · 3% Nomad Family
route3.tagline: Become a true nomad at 3,600m on the Yellow River grasslands
route3.description: Venture deep into the Zoige-Hongyuan grasslands (N33°21′ E102°10′, altitude 3,500–3,600m) — home to the Orenda nomadic camp and the global 3% who still live as nomads. Milk yaks at dawn, churn butter tea, sleep in a black yak-hair tent, and ride across the Yellow River's first great bend. Supported by Bliss Mobil 4×4 expedition vehicles. As featured on CCTV and Discovery Channel.
highlights: Nomadic Family Homestay · Yak Milking · Butter Tea
Black Tent Camping · Fireside Under the Stars
Plateau Horse Riding · Yellow River Bend Gallop
As Featured on CCTV / Discovery Channel

4.label: Nomad Between Earth & Sky (4-day sample itinerary)

days.title: Chengdu → NW Sichuan Nomadic Camp
days.desc: Depart Chengdu in the morning, heading north along the Min River valley through Wenchuan and Li County onto the NW Sichuan plateau. As the elevation rises to 3,500m, the scenery transforms from city towers to alpine meadows dotted with yak herds. Arrive in the afternoon at the Orenda nomadic camp (N33°21′ E102°10′). Receive a traditional khata welcome, meet your nomadic family, and settle into your black tent. In the evening, gather around the stove for your first bowl of butter tea and listen to the herders' stories of the grasslands and the Yellow River.

days.title: Yaks · Grasslands · A Nomad's Day
days.desc: A full day immersed in nomadic life. Rise early to milk yaks alongside the herders — the daily rhythm of every Tibetan pastoralist. Learn to churn butter tea and knead tsampa, and discover the meaning of '3% Nomad Family' — only 3% of the world's population still lives the nomadic way. In the morning, follow the herders onto the grasslands to find salt licks and tend the yaks. In the afternoon, ride horseback across the vast grasslands of the Yellow River bend — an endless sea of grass meeting the sky. At dusk, help round up the yaks. After nightfall, naro band performs under the stars, and the herders recount the Epic of King Gesar around the fire.

days.title: Grassland Gathering · Nomadic Crafts
days.desc: The liveliest day on the grasslands. If your visit coincides with a horse-racing festival, wedding, or Dharma assembly, you will take part as family: wear a Tibetan robe, drink barley wine, and dance the Guozhuang. In the morning, follow the Yellow River bend to its upper-reach coordinates (N33°21′ E102°10′) — where the world's last 3% nomadic culture meets the cradle of Yellow River civilization. In the afternoon, learn traditional nomadic crafts — spinning yak-wool yarn, braiding black-tent rope, making air-dried yak meat and traditional yogurt. In the evening, a Bliss Mobil expedition vehicle takes you deep into the grasslands for panoramic sunset views of the Yellow River bend.

days.title: Grassland Sunrise → Chengdu
days.desc: Wake early for one last grassland sunrise — at Zoige-Hongyuan, the morning sun turns the meadows gold as smoke curls from the black tents. Share a final breakfast with your nomadic family — tsampa, butter tea, fresh yak milk. Embrace and exchange contacts — from now on, you have a home on the grasslands. Return to Chengdu via Zhegu Mountain and Miyaluo, arriving in the afternoon.

faq.q: How fit do I need to be for this trip?
faq.a: Reasonably mobile is enough. There is no trekking — the expedition vehicles cover the ground. The real challenge is altitude, so we keep the schedule unhurried and build in rest.

faq.q: What are the sleeping arrangements?
faq.a: Three nights in a traditional black yak-hair tent at the nomadic camp, at roughly 3,600 m. Bedding is provided and the tents are warm, but facilities are simple: shared washing areas and no en-suite bathrooms.

faq.q: Is there electricity, phone signal and hot water?
faq.a: The camp has limited solar power for charging small devices. Mobile signal is patchy and there is no reliable data. Hot water is provided on request rather than from a running tap. Expect to disconnect — most guests find that is the point.

faq.q: What if I feel unwell at 3,600 m?
faq.a: We carry oxygen and a first-aid kit, and our team is experienced at recognising altitude sickness. If symptoms are serious we descend toward Hongyuan or Chengdu immediately. Tell your guide the moment you feel unwell rather than waiting.

faq.q: Is the departure date fixed?
faq.a: The listed dates are a sample. We run this journey on flexible dates for private groups, and it works best from June to September when the family is in their summer camp and the grasslands are green.

faq.label: Good to know
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do I need a permit to travel from Chengdu into Tibetan areas?
faq.a1: For most of Western Sichuan - Kangding, Tagong, Xinduqiao, Litang, Daocheng Yading and Danba - no special permit is required; a valid Chinese visa or visa-free entry is enough. Permits are only needed if you enter the Tibet Autonomous Region (Lhasa, Shigatse, Nyingchi), and those are arranged through a licensed Tibetan travel agency. We will tell you clearly which one applies to your route.
faq.q2: What is the best time of year for a Western Sichuan tour?
faq.a2: May to October is the main season, with the clearest skies and warmest days. Late March to April brings apricot and peach blossoms through the river valleys; June to August is greenest with the best grassland conditions; September to October gives the sharpest mountain views and golden larch. Winter trips are possible on lower routes such as Kangding and Danba, with far fewer visitors.
faq.q3: How do I handle altitude sickness on a Sichuan-Tibet route?
faq.a3: We build the itinerary upward gradually - starting at Chengdu (500m), then Kangding (2,560m), then higher passes - so your body acclimatises over several days. We carry oxygen in the vehicle, keep the pace flexible, and avoid abrupt gains above 4,000m. Most travellers adjust within a day or two; tell your guide immediately if you feel unwell and we will adjust the plan.
faq.q4: How small are the groups, and can I book a private trip?
faq.a4: Our scheduled departures run with 2 to 8 travellers, which keeps us light enough for small guesthouses and quiet monasteries that large coaches cannot reach. If you prefer your own dates and pace we run private departures for solo travellers, couples, families and friend groups all year round.
faq.q5: What does a Western Sichuan tour typically cost, and what is included?
faq.a5: Every route lists a price per person, and travel-accident insurance is included in the price: the Tibetan walking tour from US$39, the Western Sichuan highland loop from US$690 (3 days) up to US$1,390 (7 days), and the nomad camp from US$999 for a group of four, down to US$875 per person at five or six guests. A standard quote covers the private vehicle and driver, an English-speaking local guide, accommodation, entrance fees to monasteries and scenic areas, and domestic travel-accident insurance including highland rescue. International flights and personal shopping are not included.
faq.q6: Can you accommodate non-English speakers or specific dietary needs?
faq.a6: Yes. Our guides speak English, Mandarin and Tibetan, and we also run trips in Spanish and Thai on request. Vegetarian, vegan, halal and gluten-free meals can be arranged along the route - just tell us at the time of booking so we can brief each guesthouse in advance.

altitude-sickness.title: Altitude sickness in Western Sichuan: how to prepare and what to do
altitude-sickness.excerpt: Most travellers feel something above 3,000 m. Here is how to arrive well, recognise the warning signs, and what actually helps — based on what we see on the road.
altitude-sickness.metaTitle: Altitude Sickness in Sichuan: Symptoms, Prevention & What to Do
altitude-sickness.metaDesc: How to prevent and manage altitude sickness in Western Sichuan and the Tibetan plateau. Real elevation figures for Chengdu, Kangding, Tagong and Litang, plus when to descend.

sections.heading: The short version
body: Almost everyone who travels into the Sichuan highlands goes above 3,000 metres at some point. Most people feel mild symptoms for a day and are fine. A small number get properly ill, and the only reliable cure is to lose elevation.

The single most useful habit is to gain height slowly. Chengdu sits at roughly 500 m. Kangding is already 2,560 m. That is a jump of two kilometres in a single day's drive, and it is the point where many people first feel it.

sections.heading: The elevations you will actually meet
body: Knowing the numbers helps you plan rest days sensibly rather than guessing.

rows: Common first overnight; mild symptoms possible
Most people notice the thin air here
Similar to Tagong, often used as a sleep stop
One of the highest towns in the world; take it easy
Drive-through only, do not linger or sleep here

sections.heading: What actually helps
body: Ascend gradually. If your itinerary allows, spend the first night at Kangding rather than pushing straight to 3,700 m. Our four-day nomad journey is built this way on purpose.
Drink more water than feels necessary. Dry plateau air plus faster breathing dehydrates you quickly, and dehydration makes altitude symptoms noticeably worse.
Skip alcohol for the first two nights. It disrupts sleep, which is exactly what your body needs to adjust.
Eat normally, even without appetite. Carbohydrates are easier to digest at altitude than heavy fatty meals.
Do not push through a headache. A mild headache is common on day one. A headache that keeps worsening despite water and rest is your signal to stop climbing.

sections.heading: Symptoms worth taking seriously
body: Mild altitude sickness feels like a hangover: headache, tiredness, poor appetite, disturbed sleep, occasional nausea. It usually settles within a day or two as your body adapts.
Seek medical help and descend if you see any of the following. These point toward fluid on the lungs or swelling in the brain, both of which are emergencies.
list: Breathlessness at rest, or a cough that will not settle
Confusion, slurred speech, or unsteadiness on your feet
Vomiting that stops you keeping water down
A headache that keeps worsening after a full day of rest

sections.heading: Medication and oxygen
body: Acetazolamide is commonly prescribed for prevention and is worth discussing with your own doctor before you travel, particularly if you have previously reacted badly to altitude. It is not a substitute for ascending slowly.

Simple painkillers handle ordinary altitude headaches well. Many vehicles carry a small oxygen canister, and hotels at higher elevations often have one; a few minutes of oxygen can relieve symptoms temporarily, but it does not acclimatise you.
If you have a heart or lung condition, or are pregnant, speak to a doctor before booking a highland itinerary. We are happy to adjust pacing or keep an itinerary below 3,000 m entirely.

sections.heading: If you are travelling with children
body: Children generally adapt at least as well as adults, but they may not articulate what is wrong. Watch for unusual irritability, drowsiness, or a child who suddenly refuses to eat. Keep the schedule loose, and treat any high pass as somewhere to pass through rather than play.

faq.q: Do I need altitude medication before arriving in Chengdu?
faq.a: No. Chengdu is around 500 m and you will not need anything there. If your itinerary goes above 3,000 m, start any preventive medication the day before you gain significant height, following your doctor's advice.

faq.q: Can I travel to Tagong or Litang if I have never been above 2,000 m?
faq.a: Yes, and many of our guests do exactly that. The key is pacing: sleep low for the first night or two, keep the first high-altitude day light, and stay hydrated. Tell us in advance and we will build in extra rest.

faq.q: Is bottled oxygen worth bringing?
faq.a: It helps for short-term relief and reassurance, but it does not speed up acclimatisation. Use it if you feel unwell, then rest and descend rather than relying on it to keep climbing.

best-time-to-visit.title: The best time to visit Western Sichuan, month by month
best-time-to-visit.excerpt: Spring flowers, summer grasslands, autumn colour and hard winter light — what each season actually looks like on the ground, and which one suits the trip you want.
best-time-to-visit.metaTitle: Best Time to Visit Western Sichuan: A Month-by-Month Guide
best-time-to-visit.metaDesc: When to travel in Western Sichuan and the Tibetan highlands. Season-by-season weather, road conditions, grassland colour and festival timing for Kangding, Tagong and Zoige.

sections.heading: The short version
body: For most travellers, late May to early October is the sweet spot. The grasslands are green, the passes are reliably open, and the days are warm enough to sit outside.
Mid-October to mid-November is the photographer's season: golden larch and poplar, sharp clear air, and far fewer people. It gets cold at night.
Winter and early spring are quiet, cheap and beautiful in a stark way, but some high passes close and many guesthouses shut.

sections.heading: Spring — March to May
body: March is still winter at altitude. Passes can close without warning and the grasslands are brown. By April the low valleys are warming up and apricot and peach blossom appears around Danba and the Dadu River valley.
May is when the season genuinely opens. Grass begins to green, days are mild, and the roads are dependable. If you want flowers without the summer crowds, aim for the second half of May.

sections.heading: Summer — June to August
body: This is peak grassland season. Tagong and the Zoige marshes are vivid green, yaks are out in numbers, and nomad families are living in their summer camps — which is what makes our nomad homestay work best in these months.
It is also the rainy season. Expect afternoon showers rather than all-day rain, and occasional landslides on the mountain roads. Mornings are usually clear, so we front-load the scenic driving.
Summer is peak domestic holiday time, especially during the July and August school breaks. Book accommodation well ahead and expect popular viewpoints to be busy at midday.

sections.heading: Autumn — September to November
body: September and early October combine green grasslands with stable weather, and are arguably the best all-round months. Skies are clearer than in summer and the rain has eased.
Mid-October onwards brings the colour change. Larch turns gold across the high valleys and the light becomes cleaner and harder. Nights drop below freezing at altitude.
The first week of October is a national holiday and the busiest travel period of the year in China. Unless you specifically want the festival atmosphere, travel either side of it.

sections.heading: Winter — December to February
body: Winter is dry, cold and extremely clear. Snow-covered peaks against deep blue sky make it a favourite for landscape photographers, and prices are at their lowest.

The trade-offs are real: some high passes close after snowfall, many family-run guesthouses shut, and daytime temperatures at 3,700 m can stay below freezing. Our nomad homestay runs only in the warmer months for this reason.
If you do travel in winter, build in slack. A closed pass can add hours to a drive, and flexibility matters more than a fixed schedule.

sections.heading: Festivals worth planning around
body: Tibetan New Year (Losar) falls in February or March depending on the lunar calendar and is the most important festival in the region. Many businesses close as families celebrate at home, but the atmosphere in towns like Kangding is extraordinary.

Horse racing festivals on the grasslands usually take place in summer, often around July or August depending on the locality. Dates vary by county and are confirmed late, so ask us if you are planning around one.
Monastery festivals with masked cham dances happen at various points in the year. These are religious ceremonies rather than performances, and visitors are welcome to watch respectfully.

faq.q: What is the single best month for a first trip?
faq.a: September. The grasslands are still green, the summer rain has passed, skies are clear and the roads are dependable. It is also less crowded than July and August.

faq.q: How cold does it get at night in summer?
faq.a: At 3,700 m, expect single digits Celsius even in July, and close to freezing on clear nights. Bring a warm mid-layer and a windproof outer shell regardless of the season.

faq.q: Is the rainy season a problem for travelling?
faq.a: Rarely. Rain usually arrives in short afternoon bursts rather than lasting all day. The genuine risk is landslides on mountain roads after heavy falls, which occasionally force a route change — we monitor conditions and adjust.

tibetan-culture-etiquette.title: Tibetan culture etiquette: a practical guide for visitors
tibetan-culture-etiquette.excerpt: Monasteries, prayer flags, offering scarves and photographing people — the small things that make a real difference to how you are received.
tibetan-culture-etiquette.metaTitle: Tibetan Culture Etiquette: Monastery Rules & Customs for Visitors
tibetan-culture-etiquette.metaDesc: How to behave respectfully in Tibetan monasteries and communities. Dress, photography, prayer flags, kata scarves, and simple customs explained for first-time visitors.

sections.heading: The principle behind the rules
body: Almost every piece of etiquette in Tibetan areas comes back to one idea: these are living communities and working religious sites, not attractions built for visitors. If you behave as a guest in someone's home and in someone's place of worship, you will get it right the vast majority of the time.
Nobody expects you to know everything. What people notice is whether you are trying.

sections.heading: In monasteries and temples
body: Walk clockwise around monasteries, stupas and prayer wheel circuits. This is the direction of circumambulation and going the other way is the most common mistake visitors make.
Remove hats inside temple halls. Do not point your feet at statues or towards monks, and avoid sitting with your feet stretched out toward an altar.
Do not touch statues, thangkas or ritual objects, and do not step over them. If you want a closer look, ask — permission is usually given gladly.

Photography inside temple halls is often prohibited and sometimes permitted for a fee. Look for signage, and when in doubt, ask before raising a camera. A monk saying no is not being unfriendly; some rooms hold consecrated objects.

sections.heading: Prayer flags
body: Prayer flags are printed with sutras and mantras, and the wind is understood to carry the blessings they hold. They are religious material, not decoration.
Do not climb on prayer flag piles for photographs, and do not take flags home as souvenirs. If flags are being raised and you are invited to help, join in — it is a genuine gesture of participation.

sections.heading: Kata, the offering scarf
body: A kata is a silk or cotton scarf given as a mark of respect and welcome. You may well receive one. Accept it with both hands, and if you are offered it around your neck, bow slightly forward.
If you wish to give a kata yourself, hold it with both hands at chest height. When offering one to a monk or an elder, it is customary to bow as you present it.

sections.heading: Photographing people
body: Always ask first, even when the answer seems obvious. A gesture toward your camera and a questioning look works perfectly well across any language barrier.
Expect some people to decline, and accept it without pushing. Nomads and older people in rural areas are more likely to say no than younger people in towns.

If you photograph someone and they ask to see the result, showing them the screen is a small kindness that almost always leads to a warmer encounter. Sending a copy later, if you can, is better still.
Be cautious about photographing pilgrims during prostration or prayer. They are engaged in devotion, and a camera in that moment can feel like an intrusion.

sections.heading: Food, tea and hospitality
body: If you are offered butter tea or tsampa, accept at least a sip or a taste. Refusing hospitality outright is read as rejection rather than a dietary preference.
Butter tea is salty rather than sweet and takes many visitors by surprise. Drinking it slowly is entirely acceptable.
When eating with a family, wait to be told where to sit, and let your host begin first. If you are given the seat of honour, accept it with a nod rather than protesting at length.
Do not touch anyone's head. In Tibetan and broader Buddhist custom the head is considered the most sacred part of the body.

sections.heading: A few practical points
body: Dress modestly at religious sites: cover shoulders and knees, and avoid very short shorts or vest tops. A light scarf in your bag solves this instantly.
Do not hand money directly to children who ask. It encourages absence from school. If you want to give something, give it to a parent, or contribute to a local school or clinic instead.
Some monasteries and regions have restrictions on photography, drones and certain areas. Regulations do change, and we will brief you on current conditions for the specific places on your itinerary.

faq.q: Do I need to be Buddhist to visit a monastery?
faq.a: Not at all. Visitors of any faith or none are welcome at most monasteries. What matters is respectful behaviour: quiet voices, modest dress, and asking before photographing.

faq.q: Is it appropriate to give donations at monasteries?
faq.a: Yes, and small notes are perfectly normal. There is usually a box near the main hall. Donations support the monastery and the monks who live there.

faq.q: Can I take photos of prayer flags?
faq.a: Yes. The sensitivity is about treatment rather than photography. Do not climb on flag piles, drape yourself in them, or take them away as souvenirs.

what-to-pack.title: What to pack for a Western Sichuan journey
what-to-pack.excerpt: A short, honest packing list built from what guests actually forget — layers, sun protection, and the small items that make high-altitude nights comfortable.
what-to-pack.metaTitle: Western Sichuan & Tibet Packing List: What to Bring
what-to-pack.metaDesc: A practical packing list for Western Sichuan and the Tibetan plateau. Layering advice, sun protection, altitude essentials, and what you can safely leave at home.

sections.heading: The one rule that matters
body: Pack in layers, not in bulk. A single day in the highlands can swing from t-shirt weather in the sun to near freezing after dark, and the same trip can cover a humid Chengdu valley and a 4,298 m pass.
Three layers — a base, an insulating mid-layer, and a windproof or waterproof outer shell — will cover nearly every condition you will meet between May and October.

sections.heading: Clothing
body: Base layers: two or three quick-drying t-shirts or long-sleeve tops. Cotton stays wet and cold, so favour merino or synthetics.
Mid-layer: a fleece or light down jacket. This is the layer you will live in during mornings and evenings.
Outer shell: a windproof, water-resistant jacket. The wind on a 4,000 m pass is the part visitors underestimate most.
Trousers: one comfortable pair for travel days and one warmer or lined pair for highland days. Avoid jeans for long drives.
A warm hat and gloves. Even in midsummer, a clear night at 3,700 m can drop close to freezing.
Comfortable walking shoes with some grip, plus sandals or easy slip-ons for guesthouses and long drives.

sections.heading: Sun and weather
body: The plateau sun is intense, and UV exposure at 3,700 m is substantially higher than at sea level. Sunburn happens fast, even on overcast days.

Bring high-factor sunscreen and reapply through the day, sunglasses with genuine UV protection, and a wide-brimmed hat or a cap with a brim. Lip balm with SPF is worth its weight — dry air cracks lips within a day or two.

sections.heading: Health and altitude
body: Any personal medication you take, in original packaging, in your carry-on rather than checked luggage. Pharmacies in highland towns are limited.
Simple painkillers for altitude headaches, plus rehydration sachets. A small first-aid kit with plasters and a basic antiseptic covers most minor issues.
If your doctor has prescribed acetazolamide, bring it and start it as advised rather than on arrival.
A water bottle you can refill. Staying hydrated genuinely reduces altitude symptoms, and you will drink more when you are not hunting for bottles.

sections.heading: Practical kit
body: A power bank. Long drives and cold nights drain phone batteries, and charging points in rural guesthouses are limited.
A universal adaptor. China uses type A, C and I sockets at 220 V.
A head torch or small torch for guesthouses and early starts.
Tissues and hand sanitiser. Many rural toilets have no paper and no running water.
A light daypack for camera gear, water and a layer on walking days.

sections.heading: What you can leave behind
body: Heavy boots. Unless you are planning serious trekking, trail shoes or sturdy trainers are enough for the walking on our itineraries.
A large suitcase. Vehicles are comfortable but boot space is finite, and a soft bag or mid-size case travels far better on highland roads.
Excessive camera equipment. The temptation to bring everything is strong, but a single versatile lens plus a spare battery will get used far more than a heavy bag.
Formal clothing. Nothing on our itineraries calls for it.

faq.q: Can I buy cold-weather gear in Chengdu?
faq.a: Yes. Chengdu has plenty of outdoor shops and a large Decathlon, and prices for basics are reasonable. If you are short on luggage space, buying layers on arrival is a practical option.

faq.q: Do I really need a down jacket in summer?
faq.a: A light down or fleece layer, yes. Daytime temperatures are pleasant, but mornings, evenings and any time above 4,000 m can be genuinely cold even in July.

faq.q: Is there somewhere to do laundry?
faq.a: Hotels in Kangding and larger towns offer laundry, though turnaround can be a day. Hand-washing quick-dry clothing in a guesthouse basin is the simpler approach on shorter trips.

chengdu-to-tibet-transport.title: Getting from Chengdu into the Tibetan highlands
chengdu-to-tibet-transport.excerpt: Driving, flying or the train — how the main options compare, how long each really takes, and which one suits the journey you have in mind.
chengdu-to-tibet-transport.metaTitle: Chengdu to Tibet & Western Sichuan: Transport Options Compared
chengdu-to-tibet-transport.metaDesc: How to travel from Chengdu into the Tibetan highlands. Overland routes on the G318, flights to Kangding and Daocheng, bus services, and what each option involves.

sections.heading: First, a clarification that matters
body: Two different destinations are often called "Tibet", and they involve very different logistics.

The Tibetan Plateau extends far beyond the Tibet Autonomous Region. Western Sichuan — Kangding, Tagong, Litang, Danba, Zoige — is ethnically and culturally Tibetan, sits on the plateau, and is reachable from Chengdu by road with no special permit.

The Tibet Autonomous Region, with Lhasa at its centre, is a separate administrative area. It requires a permit arranged through a licensed agency, and independent travel is not permitted. If Lhasa is your goal, plan for a guided tour and allow several weeks for the paperwork.
Most travellers who want mountains, monasteries and nomad culture find that Western Sichuan delivers it without the permits or the altitude shock of flying straight to 3,650 m.

sections.heading: Overland from Chengdu
body: The classic route runs west from Chengdu on the G318, the Sichuan–Tibet highway, climbing through Ya'an and over the Erlang Shan range to Kangding.

Driving time from Chengdu to Kangding is roughly five to seven hours depending on traffic leaving the city and conditions on the pass. From Kangding onwards the road continues to Xinduqiao, Tagong and eventually Litang.

This is the option we recommend for most guests. The gradual ascent gives your body time to adapt, the scenery builds progressively, and you can stop where you like rather than watching it pass from a plane window.
Distances look short on a map and are not. Mountain roads average perhaps 40–50 km/h, and a landslide or roadworks can add hours. Build slack into any self-drive plan.

sections.heading: Flying
body: Kangding has an airport at roughly 4,280 m, and Daocheng Yading has one at around 4,410 m. Both are among the highest commercial airports in the world.

Flying gets you there in about an hour, but it drops you at very high altitude with no acclimatisation at all. A significant proportion of travellers who fly directly to either airport feel unwell on arrival, sometimes badly enough to spend the first day in bed.
If you do fly, treat the first day as a rest day. Do not schedule a high pass or a long drive. Drink water, eat lightly, and sleep early.

sections.heading: Bus and shared minivan
body: Regular buses run from Chengdu's Chadianzi and Xinnanmen stations to Kangding, and onward services reach Tagong and Litang. They are cheap and reliable.
Shared minivans fill the gap for smaller places and leave when full rather than on a schedule. They are the standard local way to move between highland towns.
The limitation is fixed timetables and no flexibility to stop for the views — which, on this road, is much of the point.

sections.heading: How we handle it
body: On our own journeys we drive, with a vehicle and driver who know the route. It means we can stop when the light is good, adjust when weather moves in, and pace the altitude gain deliberately rather than by timetable.
For guests arriving from overseas we usually suggest a night in Chengdu first. It costs one day, it resets your body clock, and it means you start the climb rested rather than jet-lagged.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to visit Western Sichuan?
faq.a: No. Kangding, Tagong, Xinduqiao, Danba and the Zoige grasslands are open to foreign visitors without a special permit. The Tibet Autonomous Region is a different matter and does require one.

faq.q: How long does the drive from Chengdu to Kangding take?
faq.a: Typically five to seven hours, depending on how quickly you clear Chengdu traffic and conditions on the mountain pass. In bad weather or after a landslide it can take considerably longer.

faq.q: Should I fly to Kangding to save time?
faq.a: Only if your schedule is very tight. The airport sits at about 4,280 m, and arriving there from sea level in an hour causes altitude symptoms for many travellers. Driving in over two days is far gentler.

first-time-tibet-travel.title: Your first trip to the Tibetan plateau: what to know before you book
first-time-tibet-travel.excerpt: Permits, altitude, timing and expectations — the decisions that shape a first journey into Tibetan country, explained without the sales pitch.
first-time-tibet-travel.metaTitle: First Time Travelling to Tibet: A Beginner's Planning Guide
first-time-tibet-travel.metaDesc: Planning a first trip to the Tibetan plateau. Permits explained, Western Sichuan versus the Tibet Autonomous Region, altitude preparation, best seasons and realistic expectations.

sections.heading: Start with one decision
body: Before anything else, decide where you mean by Tibet. The answer changes your permits, your budget, your itinerary and how much freedom you have.

Western Sichuan is culturally Tibetan, sits on the plateau, and is open to independent travel. The Tibet Autonomous Region around Lhasa requires a permit, a licensed guide and a fixed itinerary. Neither is better; they are simply different trips.

If you are drawn to monasteries, grasslands, nomad families and high mountain roads, Western Sichuan offers all of it with far less bureaucracy. If Lhasa and the Potala Palace are the point, plan for the permit route.

sections.heading: Permits, briefly
body: For the Tibet Autonomous Region, foreign travellers need a Tibet Travel Permit arranged through a licensed agency. You cannot apply directly, and you cannot travel independently once there — a guide accompanies you throughout.

Processing takes time and is not guaranteed. Certain nationalities and certain periods, particularly around sensitive anniversaries, face additional scrutiny. Apply well ahead and keep your plans flexible.
For Western Sichuan, none of this applies. Bring your passport, and be aware that some individual monasteries or areas may occasionally restrict photography.

sections.heading: Altitude is the thing to respect
body: This is the part first-time visitors most often underestimate, and it is the part that ruins trips when ignored.
Lhasa sits at 3,650 m. Tagong is 3,700 m. Litang is 4,014 m. Arriving at any of these from sea level is a genuine physical shock, and the effects do not care how fit you are.

The fix is simple and unglamorous: gain height gradually, drink more water than feels reasonable, skip alcohol for the first nights, and do not schedule anything ambitious on your first high-altitude day.
See our dedicated altitude guide for the full picture.

sections.heading: When to go
body: Late May to early October is the reliable window, with September standing out for clear skies, green grasslands and manageable crowds.
Winter travel is possible and can be spectacular, but passes close, guesthouses shut, and flexibility becomes essential rather than optional.
Avoid the first week of October unless you actively want China's busiest travel period. Accommodation prices spike and popular sites are crowded.

sections.heading: What it will actually feel like
body: Expect long drives. Distances on the plateau are measured in hours rather than kilometres, and a route that looks short on a map can take most of a day.
Expect basic infrastructure in rural areas. Guesthouses in nomad areas are comfortable but simple, hot water may be limited, and mobile signal comes and goes.

Expect the unexpected to be handled calmly. Weather closes passes, festivals shift dates, and roads need repairs. The travellers who enjoy the plateau most are the ones who treat the plan as a direction rather than a contract.
And expect moments that justify all of it: sunrise light on a snow peak, butter tea in a nomad tent, a monastery courtyard at dawn with nobody else there.

sections.heading: A realistic first itinerary
body: If you have a week and want to do this well: two nights in Chengdu to adjust and see the city, then west over the pass with a first night at Kangding, then on to Tagong and Xinduqiao for the highland scenery, then back down.
That gives you genuine Tibetan culture, real altitude, and time to breathe, without the punishing pace of trying to reach Lhasa overland in the same week.

faq.q: Is Western Sichuan a good substitute for Lhasa?
faq.a: It is a different experience rather than a substitute. Western Sichuan gives you Tibetan culture, monasteries, grasslands and nomad life with far more freedom and no permit requirements. Lhasa offers the Potala Palace and the major monastic centres, at the cost of a guided, fixed itinerary.

faq.q: How fit do I need to be?
faq.a: Reasonably mobile is enough for our itineraries. There is no technical trekking. The challenge is altitude rather than exertion, and pacing matters far more than fitness.

faq.q: How far ahead should I plan?
faq.a: For Western Sichuan, a few weeks is usually plenty, more if you want specific accommodation in peak summer. For the Tibet Autonomous Region, allow at least two to three months for permits and paperwork.

tibet-permit-explained.title: Do you need a Tibet permit for Western Sichuan?
tibet-permit-explained.excerpt: The single most common question we get from foreign travellers — and the answer surprises almost everyone. If your trip stays in Sichuan, you do not need a Tibet permit. Here is exactly where the line falls.
tibet-permit-explained.metaTitle: Tibet Permit for Western Sichuan? What You Need
tibet-permit-explained.metaDesc: Do you need a Tibet permit for Kangding, Tagong or Danba? No — Western Sichuan needs only a China visa. Here is where the permit line actually falls.

sections.heading: The short answer
body: If your itinerary stays inside Sichuan Province — Chengdu, Kangding, Xinduqiao, Tagong, Danba, Siguniang Mountain, the Zoige and Hongyuan grasslands — you do not need a Tibet Travel Permit.

You need a valid Chinese visa (or visa-free entry, depending on your nationality), your passport, and nothing else in the way of special paperwork. All three of our routes are entirely within Sichuan.

sections.heading: Why this confuses almost everyone
body: The confusion is understandable, and it is not the traveller’s fault. Two entirely different places both get called "Tibet" in English.

The first is the Tibet Autonomous Region, usually shortened to TAR — the area administered from Lhasa, covering roughly the western half of the Tibetan plateau. This is the Tibet of Everest Base Camp, Lhasa and Shigatse. Entry here requires a Tibet Travel Permit, and foreign travellers must also join an organised tour with a licensed guide for the whole duration.

The second is the Tibetan cultural world outside the TAR. The Tibetan plateau spills far beyond the TAR’s borders into Sichuan, Qinghai, Gansu and Yunnan. These areas are historically and culturally Tibetan, and the people living there are Tibetan — but they are administratively part of those other provinces, and they are not the TAR.
Western Sichuan is entirely in the second category. When a tour is called "Tibetan Sichuan", "Kham" or "Eastern Tibet", it almost always means this second kind.

sections.heading: Where the line actually falls
body: The practical rule is administrative, not cultural. A place inside the Tibet Autonomous Region needs a permit. A place outside it does not.
Everything in the table below is in Sichuan and needs no permit:

sections.heading: What you do need for Western Sichuan
body: A valid passport with at least six months’ validity remaining, and a current Chinese visa — or entry under a visa-free arrangement if your nationality qualifies.

Carry your passport with you on the road. Scenic areas, some hotels and a number of checkpoints in Ganzi and Aba prefectures will ask to see it. Keep a photo of your passport and visa on your phone as a backup.
That is the entire list. There is no additional permit to apply for, no agency paperwork, and no minimum group size for Western Sichuan.

sections.heading: What changes if you extend into the TAR
body: If you later decide to continue west from Sichuan into the Tibet Autonomous Region — for example Chengdu overland to Lhasa on the G318 — the rules change completely at the border, and they are considerably stricter.

You will need a Tibet Travel Permit, which can only be arranged through a licensed Tibetan travel agency, not applied for directly. You must travel with an organised tour and a licensed guide for the whole time you are inside the TAR. Independent travel is not permitted for foreign visitors.
Processing takes time and the permit is issued for specific dates against a fixed itinerary. It cannot be obtained at short notice, and you cannot simply turn up at the boundary and buy one.
This is worth knowing early, because it is easy to assume a long overland trip needs a permit from day one. It does not — only the TAR portion does.

sections.heading: One honest caveat
body: Permit policy is administrative and it does change. Areas that have been open can close temporarily for conservation, weather, road works or local restrictions, and notice is sometimes short.

For any of our Sichuan routes this is a non-issue, because the permit question simply does not arise. But if your wider plans include the TAR, always confirm the current position with a licensed agency shortly before you travel rather than relying on a guide written months earlier.

faq.q: Do I need a Tibet permit to visit Kangding, Tagong or Danba?
faq.a: No. All three are in Sichuan Province, not the Tibet Autonomous Region. A valid Chinese visa and your passport are all you need. There is no additional permit and no minimum group size.

faq.q: Is "Tibetan Sichuan" the same as Tibet?
faq.a: No. Western Sichuan is culturally Tibetan and home to many Tibetan communities, but it is administratively part of Sichuan Province. The Tibet Autonomous Region is a separate administrative area administered from Lhasa, and that is where a Tibet Travel Permit applies.

faq.q: Can I travel independently in Western Sichuan?
faq.a: Yes. Unlike the Tibet Autonomous Region, Western Sichuan places no requirement on foreign visitors to join an organised tour. You can travel independently, hire a driver, or join a small group — it is entirely your choice.

faq.q: What if I want to continue from Sichuan into the Tibet Autonomous Region?
faq.a: Then you will need a Tibet Travel Permit, arranged in advance through a licensed Tibetan travel agency, and you must travel with an organised tour and licensed guide throughout the TAR. Independent travel is not permitted there for foreign visitors.

faq.q: How far in advance should I arrange a permit if I do need one?
faq.a: Allow several weeks at minimum, and more in peak season. Permits are issued against specific dates and a fixed itinerary, so late applications and last-minute changes are difficult. For our Sichuan-only routes, none of this applies.

faq.q: Do I need to carry my passport in Western Sichuan?
faq.a: Yes, carry it. Scenic areas, some hotels and various checkpoints in Ganzi and Aba prefectures may ask to see it. Keep a phone photo of your passport and visa as a backup.

about.subtitle: Chengdu Journeys runs small-group trips from Chengdu into the Tibetan highlands of Western Sichuan. We are a small team, we keep groups small, and we travel the routes we built.
story: Placeholder — replace this section with your own story. What brought you to this work, how the first journey came together, and what you wanted to do differently from the tours you had seen.

A few sentences written plainly will do more than polished marketing copy. Readers are trying to work out whether they trust you with a week of their holiday, and the honest version of how you started is the most persuasive thing on this page.
If there is a specific moment that set it off — a place, a person, a trip that went wrong and taught you something — that is the detail worth keeping.
